original: % Scriptural material related to the Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālaśaṃvara amounts to two titles, which are to be found in the sDe dge canon in volume Ka of the Rgyud section (Tōh. nos. 366 and 367) [= Peking Rgyud Ka, Ōtani nos. 8 and 9]. The first is the tantra in question in ten chapters (here referred to as an *uttaratantra - probably by error), whereas the second is the *Sarvakalpasamuccaya (here referred to as an *uttarottaratantra) in five chapters (numbered 18 to 22). The latter too must be an original Indic work, since we have a commentary on it by Ānandagarbha, and some testimonia (quoted [not yet traced] and referred to once each in the Caryāmelāpakapradīpa and the Tattvasiddhi). According to the testimony of *Pramuditavajra (see below) and Bu ston Rin chen grub, there existed yet another tantra of this cycle in seven chapters. Bu ston even states that there were in his time (early 14th century) rumours of an early translation of this text, but that it cannot be found anymore (\textit{\ldots\ sngar 'gyur par grags te da lta ma rnyed do ||}). This, apparently, would account for the strange numeration of the *Sarvakalpasamuccaya, since seven chapters make up the gap between the ten chapters of the root-tantra, and the first—numbered eighteenth—of the continuation-tantra.

original: % Tōh. 1663 [= Ōta. 2535] is another *pañjikā, by one *Praśāntamitra. He is probably not to be confused with the translator under the same name. Tradition stemming from India identify him as a student of Jñānapāda, and a contemporary of Dīpaṃkarabhadra. His floruit thus most likely falls somewhere in the middle of the ninth century. He is also a commentator of the Māyājāla (Tōh. 2514) and the Vajramaṇḍālaṃkāra (Tōh. 2515) (the dedication verses are very similar to the one in the commentary relevant here; all three most likely contained the phrase `saha praśāntamitreṇa'). For the time being I cannot find any quoted or referred text in his work that would place him any time later than the range proposed above.

original: % Tōh. 1664-1671 [= Ōta. 2536-2543] are all attributed to the siddha Kukurāja; these are sādhanas and an initiation manual. It is noteworthy that the latter also speaks of the Fourth Initiation. Tōh. 1672 [= Ōta. 2544] is a *gaṇa[cakra]vidhi attributed to (an) Indrabhūti. This work has been partially translated and studied to some extent by Davidson (2002: ~318-319). The remaining texts are all sādhanas, most of which are attributed to one *Hūṃkāravajra (and variants of this name). An exception is another initiation manual, Tōh. no. 1679 [= Ōta. 2551], which is attributed to one *Ratnavajra, possibly the same as the eleventh-century Kashmiri author. I would not favour this identification, since this *Ratnavajra discusses and endorses the Fourth Initiation, whereas we know from the Kashmiri *Ratnavajra's other works and testimonia that he was not ready to accept its existence and vigorously debated `Eastern paṇḍitas' (by which he meant, first and foremost, Vāgīśvarakīrti) who were, at least to him, its chief proponents. It is noteable that this *Ratnavajra states in the second introductory verse that (by his time) the tantra and its system has become almost extinct (\textit{kun du nub po nyid mthong nas}), which is one of the reasons for his writing the manual.
